story: Meet GJ 1214 b, the exoplanet that pulled a bait-and-switch on NASA. Discovered in 2009 roughly 40 to 48 light-years away, this "sub-Neptune" spent over a decade hiding behind a thick, featureless fog. Because of its low density, early models suggested a "waterworld"—a planet made of 75% ice and steam. It was even formally named "Enaiposha," the Maasai word for a large body of water. But the James Webb Space Telescope just shattered that image. By tracking the planet through a full 38-hour orbit, JWST pierced the haze to find a "Super-Venus" instead. The planet is a gleaming, metallic pressure cooker choked with carbon dioxide. It is so reflective it shines like a mirror in space, proving that this "ocean world" is actually a high-pressure chemical oven. Instead of a tropical sea, GJ 1214 b is a class of planet entirely alien to our solar system.
angle: For years, astronomers called GJ 1214 b a "waterworld" made of 75% ice, but the James Webb Space Telescope recently revealed it's actually a "Super-Venus" choked with metallic carbon dioxide.
